A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LP-based conformal prediction work and contain readable text, equations and figures. V1's inline proofs match material relocated to v2's Appendix C; the new Appendices A–B are also available for comparison.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original coverage and prediction-set-size experiments on MNIST, ImageNet and iWildCam, including simulated perturbations and real distribution shifts.

after.justification: Section 5 retains original empirical evaluations and expands the comparisons. Appendix A adds experimental results for estimating LP ambiguity-set parameters.

M1.justification: V2 introduces Algorithm 1 for estimating LP parameters, where v1 used specified parameters or manual exploration. It computes empirical LP distances across an epsilon grid, evaluates worst-case quantiles using a separate calibration batch, and selects the smallest quantile. This adds a substantive parameter-selection procedure requiring shifted test scores.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate MNIST and ImageNet under the same three combinations of input noise and label corruption, plus iWildCam's camera-location/time shifts. The added estimator evaluations use these retained datasets and scenarios.

E2.justification: Figure 3 expands the evaluated comparator set from standard conformal prediction and chi-square robust conformal prediction to include Weight, RSCP and FG-CP. These are actual reported comparisons on MNIST and ImageNet, not merely additional citations.

E3.justification: V1 empirically tunes the chi-square radius separately for each perturbation setting; v2 instead reports slab estimation in Appendix B. The new LP-estimation experiments introduce separate calibration batches, shifted test-score samples and grid-based selection. The newly disclosed 1000/5000 calibration/test counts do not establish that existing sample sizes changed.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of whether automatic parameter selection achieves efficient coverage: Figures 5–6 examine candidate parameter pairs and their worst-case quantiles, while Figure 4 compares estimated parameters with exhaustive grid selection on iWildCam. These extend v1's parameter heatmaps into an empirical assessment of the estimation procedure.

E5.justification: Both versions report individual calibration-test split outcomes and means across 30 splits in Figure 3. V2 introduces no new reported seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or experimental uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: V1 reports valid chi-square coverage throughout Figure 3; v2 reports undercoverage at stronger shifts after changing its radius-selection procedure, so this is not a same-setting decline. V2 also adds results for three baselines and estimated LP parameters. For example, Figure 5 reports ImageNet coverage 0.91 and set size 10.69 at p=0.05, u=1.0.

T1.justification: The existing LP propositions, coverage theorem, corollaries and proofs are retained, with proofs relocated to Appendix C. Appendix A newly argues that empirical parameter estimation with disjoint calibration batches preserves coverage through Corollary 4.2. This adds a validity argument, but no new theorem or error bound establishes that extension.

C1.justification: The abstract and three introductory contributions retain the same central claims about LP modeling, score propagation and robust conformal prediction. However, Section 5.2's closing takeaways now claim that estimated parameters match grid-tuned coverage and efficiency, replacing v1's proposal to develop automated estimation in future work.

C2.justification: V2 attributes competing methods' coverage failures to violated absolute continuity, expanding v1's discussion of radius-selection difficulties. It also clarifies the limited role of Lipschitzness, discusses parameter sensitivity, and explicitly acknowledges that estimation requires shifted test scores and that ordinary conformal prediction may be preferable when such data are available.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies calibration/test counts, A100 hardware, estimator grid and sample sizes, transport-solver options, and baseline implementation details, including density-ratio estimation. The reproduction repository remains unchanged. V1's statement about image normalization by empirical means and standard deviations is omitted.

R1.justification: Section 1.1 substantially expands comparisons with semiparametric covariate-shift methods, fine-grained robust inference, Wasserstein-regularized conformal prediction and confounding-sensitivity approaches. These additions explain substantive relationships and distinctions beyond the earlier reweighting/ambiguity-set/sequential-learning overview.

P1.justification: V2 reorganizes the manuscript by moving the inline proofs to Appendix C and baseline formulas to Appendix B, while substantially rewriting the experimental narrative and expanding related work. It adds an estimation appendix and corrects the duplicated propagation-proposition numbering.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is extensively redesigned to display seven methods, with stacked coverage/size panels and broken size axes. Figure 4 adds estimated and grid-selected parameter markers and annotations. Figures 5–6 and Algorithm 1 are new displays; Figures 1–2 are substantially retained.

improvement.justification: Broader comparisons, explicit implementation details and estimator diagnostics make v2 more informative and reproducible than v1's largely manual parameter treatment. The gain is tempered by Appendix A's claim of preserved coverage without an argument controlling population-shift estimation error or parameter selection. The revised chi-square findings also depend on changed tuning. Thus practical assessment improves, but the new estimator's asserted guarantee remains insufficiently supported.
